cues.text: Welcome to Periodic Trends.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
The modern periodic law connects recurring properties with atomic number, not
merely atomic mass.
Increasing nuclear charge determines the electron count of a neutral atom,
while recurring outer configurations explain many similarities.
Period number usually identifies the highest occupied principal shell in a
ground state main group atom.
Sodium ends in three s one, placing it in period three and group one.
Chlorine ends in three s two, three p five, placing it in period three and
group seventeen.
Electronic blocks describe the kind of subshell receiving the differentiating
electron.
Sodium is s block and chlorine is p block.
Helium has one s two, so its configuration is s type, yet its closed shell
chemistry places it in group eighteen with noble gases.
Do not confuse electronic block with group placement.
Transition and inner transition series require care because their filling
subshells are not the outermost principal shell.
Elements in the same group can still differ in their chemical reactions.
An electron feels attraction to the nucleus and repulsion from other
electrons.
Effective nuclear charge is a model for the net nuclear attraction experienced
by a particular electron after shielding is considered.
It is not automatically atomic number minus every other electron: shielding
effectiveness depends on orbital distribution.
Inner electrons generally shield an outer electron more effectively than
electrons in the same shell.
Across a typical main group period, protons are added while electrons enter
the
same principal shell, so shielding does not fully cancel the increased nuclear
charge.
The outer cloud generally contracts.
Down a group, additional occupied shells increase typical distance and
shielding; the outer size generally grows despite more protons.
Penetration also matters: within a shell, an s orbital samples regions nearer
the nucleus more strongly than a p orbital in the usual qualitative
comparison.
This helps explain subshell energy differences in many electron atoms.
Use these competing effects to explain a trend before memorizing an arrow.
A qualitative effective charge argument is not a numerical calculation unless
a
specific model is supplied.
Atomic radius is inferred from distances, so its definition matters.
A covalent radius is commonly based on a bonded internuclear distance, while a
van der Waals radius describes nonbonded contact.
Metallic radii use distances in metallic structures.
Do not compare a noble gas nonbonded radius with a neighbouring element's
covalent radius and treat the difference as a simple exception to one
identical
measurement.
Within a consistent set, main group atomic radii generally decrease across a
period and increase down a group.
A positive ion is usually smaller than its neutral parent because electrons
are
removed and attraction per remaining electron increases; losing an entire
outer
shell makes the contraction especially strong.
A negative ion is usually larger because added electrons increase repulsion in
the cloud.
Sodium ion is smaller than sodium atom, whereas chloride ion is larger than
chlorine atom.
Ionic radius values also depend on coordination and the structural convention
used to assign them.
Always identify whether the question compares atoms, ions or an isoelectronic
series before ranking sizes.
Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons.
That common count makes nuclear charge a useful comparison, provided the
species are being compared on a consistent basis.
Oxygen two minus has eight protons and ten electrons.
Fluoride has nine protons and ten electrons.
Sodium plus has eleven protons and ten electrons, while magnesium two plus has
twelve protons and ten electrons.
The radius decreases in that order because increasing nuclear charge pulls the
common electron population inward more strongly.
Thus oxide is largest and magnesium two plus smallest in this set.
Do the subtraction explicitly: electron count equals atomic number minus
signed
ionic charge.
A negative charge therefore adds electrons.
Do not compare raw charge labels without checking which element is involved.
An ion with a larger positive charge is not automatically smaller than every
other ion in the periodic table, because different occupied shells can
dominate.
For another ten electron member, aluminium three plus has thirteen protons and
lies smaller than magnesium two plus in the same qualitative sequence.
This reasoning concerns size, not which isolated ion is easiest to produce.
First ionization energy removes one electron from an isolated gaseous atom in
its ground state.
It is positive for this process.
Across a typical main group period it generally increases, and down a group it
generally decreases, but electronic details produce important exceptions.
Beryllium has a filled two s subshell, whereas boron loses its first two p
electron.
That higher energy, less penetrating electron is easier to remove, so
beryllium
has the larger first ionization energy.
Nitrogen has three singly occupied two p orbitals.
Oxygen introduces a pair into one of them, and removal of a paired electron
relieves repulsion.
Nitrogen therefore has the larger first ionization energy despite oxygen's
greater nuclear charge.
Similar reasoning helps with magnesium versus aluminium and phosphorus versus
sulfur.
These explanations refine the broad trend; they do not justify ignoring all
nuclear attraction effects.
Ionization energy is not the energy needed to break a chemical bond, nor the
tendency to attract shared electrons.
Write the gas phase electron removal process before deciding which quantity a
question asks about.
Successive ionization energies refer to removing electrons one at a time from
increasingly positive gaseous ions.
The second removes an electron from a singly positive ion, not another fresh
neutral atom.
Successive removal generally costs more, and a particularly large jump can
identify when an inner closed shell must be disrupted.
Magnesium has a neon core followed by three s two.
Removing two outer electrons gives the neon like magnesium two plus ion.
The third ionization then removes a core electron, so the major jump is
between
the second and third values.
Sodium has only one outer three s electron and shows its core related jump
after the first removal.
In simple main group comparisons this connects configurations with common
ionic
charges.
However, oxidation state is formal electron bookkeeping in a compound, not
proof that free ions with those charges exist.
Chlorine often has minus one in chlorides but can have positive oxidation
states in oxygen compounds; fluorine has minus one in its compounds.
Group similarity does not mean a single allowed oxidation state for every
member.
For electron gain enthalpy, write a gaseous atom plus an electron forming a
gaseous negative ion.
If energy is released, the enthalpy change is negative under this convention.
Some electron affinity tables instead report the positive magnitude of
released
energy.
Read the sign convention before ordering values.
Chlorine has a more negative first electron gain enthalpy than fluorine.
Fluorine's compact two p electron cloud produces stronger repulsion for the
incoming electron, so the simple expectation from atomic size alone fails.
Adding a second electron to an already negative isolated gaseous ion requires
energy because the incoming electron encounters repulsion.
Formation of a stable ionic solid can still be favourable when the entire
energy cycle, including lattice formation, is considered.
Electronegativity is different: it describes an atom's attraction for shared
electron density in a bond on a chosen scale.
Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine even though chlorine's first
electron gain is more exothermic.
Keep process energies, sign conventions and bond based scales in separate
columns.
Metallic character generally decreases across a main group period and
increases
down a group.
This supports broad changes in oxide behaviour.
Across period three, sodium oxide and magnesium oxide are basic, aluminium
oxide is amphoteric, and several nonmetal oxides are acidic.
Amphoteric means reacting with both acids and bases under suitable conditions;
it does not mean the oxide has no acid base chemistry.
Do not extend a broad trend to every oxidation state or every oxide without
checking the compound.
Alkali metals generally become easier to ionize down the group, but a measured
reaction depends on more than ionization alone.
Hydration energies, bond breaking, physical state and kinetics can change
comparisons.
Halogen oxidizing strength in ordinary aqueous chemistry broadly decreases
down
the group, yet electron gain enthalpy by itself cannot supply the full
explanation.
For a ranking question, first identify the property, then compare
configurations, shells and the relevant process.
Finally inspect known exceptions and conditions.
The practice questions combine those steps; further group chemistry and
detailed transition element trends require separate study.
Successive ionization data can reveal a valence pattern when a much larger
energy is required after the outer electrons have been removed.
Take supplied values five hundred seventy eight, one thousand eight hundred
seventeen, two thousand seven hundred forty five and eleven thousand five
hundred seventy seven kilojoules per mole.
The conspicuous jump is between the third and fourth removals.
In a suitable main group interpretation this suggests three outer electrons
before a more tightly bound inner shell is reached.
It is consistent with group thirteen behaviour, but these four values alone
are
not a general proof of an exact atomic number.
Each successive ionization starts from a different, more positively charged
gaseous ion, so the terms are not repeated removals from an unchanged neutral
atom.
To form the triply charged gaseous ion from the neutral gaseous atom, add the
first three energies, giving five thousand one hundred forty.
Do not use only the third energy for the whole process.
Configuration, periodic position and the stated model should support the
assignment, especially when transition elements or unusual electronic states
are possible.
Electron gain enthalpy describes the energy change when a gaseous species
accepts an electron.
Under the enthalpy change convention, an exothermic addition has a negative
value.
A table of electron affinity may instead report a positive magnitude for
energy
released, so the same physical event can appear with a different sign
convention.
Read the defining reaction and heading first.
Suppose illustrative first electron gain enthalpies are minus three hundred
twenty eight for fluorine and minus three hundred forty nine kilojoules per
mole for chlorine.
Chlorine releases more energy in this comparison, despite fluorine being
higher
in the group.
The compact fluorine valence shell produces stronger repulsions for the added
electron.
Now distinguish adding an electron to a neutral oxygen atom from adding
another
to an oxygen anion.
The second addition faces electrostatic repulsion and is endothermic for the
isolated gaseous ion.
The existence of oxide ions in solids does not contradict that fact: lattice
formation and other steps contribute to the overall thermodynamic cycle.
One electron gain term alone cannot decide whether an entire ionic compound
forms.
An atomic radius is an operational description, not a sharply defined surface
around an electron cloud.
A covalent radius can be obtained from half the internuclear distance between
identical bonded atoms.
If a supplied homonuclear single bond distance is one hundred ninety eight
picometres, that convention gives ninety nine picometres for the atom.
A van der Waals radius uses nonbonded contacts and is usually larger for the
same element.
Metallic and ionic radii come from other structural environments.
An ionic radius also depends on the stated coordination and oxidation state
convention.
Therefore a ranking that mixes a noble gas van der Waals value with a
neighbour's covalent value can produce an apparent exception that reflects the
measurement definition.
Within a consistent isoelectronic series, increasing nuclear charge commonly
contracts the electronic distribution; within one element, a cation is
generally smaller than its neutral atom under suitable comparisons.
These useful trends do not remove the need to compare compatible datasets.
Check charge, electron count, coordination environment and radius definition
before explaining a small numerical difference as a new periodic law.
Oxide acid base classification should be supported by the actual compound and
a
balanced reaction.
Sodium oxide reacts with hydrochloric acid to form sodium chloride and water:
one sodium oxide requires two hydrogen chloride units.
Aluminium oxide can react with acid as well.
One aluminium oxide plus six hydrogen chloride units forms two aluminium
chloride units and three waters in a simplified formula equation.
Under suitable aqueous strongly basic conditions, aluminium oxide can form
tetrahydroxoaluminate.
A balanced representation uses one aluminium oxide, two hydroxide ions and
three waters to form two tetrahydroxoaluminate ions.
This acid and base behaviour supports the word amphoteric.
It does not mean the oxide is neutral or reacts equally rapidly under
arbitrary
conditions.
Silicon dioxide can show acidic oxide behaviour through reactions with
suitable
strong bases, while conditions and product conventions must be stated.
Oxidation state matters too: different oxides of the same element need not
share one classification.
Use a broad across period trend to organize examples, then check the actual
chemistry rather than treating a left to right arrow as a substitute for an
equation.
A gas phase ionization trend does not by itself determine the reducing
strength
of a metal in aqueous standard conditions.
Converting a solid metal to an aqueous cation involves atomization, ionization
and hydration contributions.
Compare the supplied standard reduction potentials for lithium, sodium and
potassium ions becoming their metals: minus three point zero four, minus two
point seven one and minus two point nine three volts respectively.
Reversing each half reaction describes metal oxidation.
In this comparison lithium has the most negative reduction potential and the
strongest standard thermodynamic reducing tendency of the three metals.
This does not follow the simple expectation obtained by looking only at how
easily a gas phase electron is removed down the group.
Strong stabilization of the small aqueous lithium ion is part of the
explanation.
These potentials do not rank the observed speed or violence of a metal
reacting
with water.
Surface condition, melting, mass transfer and reaction pathways affect that
observation.
Keep thermodynamic tendency, individual energy terms and reaction rate
distinct.
Use the stated solvent and standard conditions; changing the medium can change
the comparison.
An electron configuration can locate a neutral main group atom when the
subshell pattern is read carefully.
Consider a supplied configuration with a neon core, two electrons in three s
and three in three p.
The largest occupied principal quantum number is three, so this atom lies in
period three.
Five electrons occupy the outer s and p subshells together, giving group
fifteen in the usual main group numbering.
The differentiating electron enters a p subshell, so it is a p block element.
The total electron count is ten plus two plus three, or fifteen; for the
neutral atom the atomic number is also fifteen.
Do not identify group three merely from the superscript on the p subshell, and
do not identify the period from the number of valence electrons.
An ion requires another step: the configuration describes its remaining
electrons, not necessarily the neutral parent atomic number.
Helium is a familiar boundary case, with a filled one s shell but placement in
group eighteen based on the periodic organization.
The simple s and p group shortcut should not be extended unchanged to
transition metal configurations.
The modern periodic table organizes elements by atomic number, not by
assigning
a separate chemical position to each isotope mass.
Consider chlorine thirty five and chlorine thirty seven, both with seventeen
protons.
Neutral atoms of each have seventeen electrons, giving the same ordinary
electron configuration pattern and the same periodic group and period.
Their neutron counts differ: eighteen for mass number thirty five and twenty
for mass number thirty seven.
A chloride ion has one extra electron, eighteen in total, but its nucleus
still
has seventeen protons.
It remains chlorine rather than turning into argon, whose nucleus has eighteen
protons.
Thus isotope formation, ion formation and changing the element are distinct
operations.
Chemical properties of isotopes are similar because of their electronic
structures, though isotope effects mean they are not identical in every
measurable process.
Mass number is the integer proton plus neutron count for a specified nuclide,
while relative atomic mass of a natural sample is an isotopic average.
Reading an average near thirty five point five as an individual atom with a
fractional neutron count would confuse these two quantities.
Always identify charge and nuclide information before counting electrons or
locating the element.
The energy of adding a second electron cannot be copied from the first
electron
gain.
For an isolated gas phase oxygen atom, the first addition makes an anion,
whereas the second addition brings another negative electron toward an already
negative ion.
The second step is generally energetically costly for forming such a multiply
charged isolated anion.
Use supplied illustrative step values of minus one hundred forty one and plus
seven hundred forty four kilojoules per mole for the first and second oxygen
electron additions.
The total energy change for forming gas phase oxide ions from gas phase oxygen
atoms and two electrons is plus six hundred three kilojoules per mole.
Thus the complete two electron gas phase process is endothermic under those
supplied values even though the first step is exothermic.
This does not mean oxide solids cannot be stable.
Formation of a solid includes other contributions, especially favourable
lattice formation, and any full formation calculation also needs the
appropriate atomization and metal ionization steps.
Keep the isolated ion process distinct from the complete solid formation
cycle.
State whether a quoted electron affinity uses an energy released convention or
an electron gain enthalpy convention before attaching a sign.
As a supporting connection to atomic energy calculations, convert an
ionization
energy without mixing particle and mole units.
Suppose a hypothetical isolated gas phase atom has first ionization threshold
five point zero zero electron volts per atom.
With the supplied conversion one electron volt per particle equals ninety six
point four eight five kilojoules per mole, the molar threshold is four hundred
eighty two point four two five kilojoules per mole.
That number is not the energy of one individual atom in kilojoules.
For a photon comparison, use the supplied relation photon energy in electron
volts equals approximately twelve hundred forty divided by wavelength in
nanometres.
A threshold of five electron volts corresponds to about two hundred forty
eight
nanometres.
A two hundred nanometre photon has about six point two electron volts,
exceeding this ideal threshold, whereas a three hundred nanometre photon has
about four point one three and is below it.
These are energy comparisons for the stipulated one photon isolated atom
model,
not predictions of an experimental ionization yield.
Cross sections, states and experimental conditions matter.
Keep the periodic trend in ionization energy separate from the unit conversion
used to express a particular supplied value.
A diagonal relationship is a selected chemical similarity between elements in
different groups, not a claim that their electron configurations are
identical.
Lithium and magnesium are a familiar supporting comparison: both can form
nitrides by direct combination with nitrogen under suitable conditions.
Lithium nitride is lithium three N, whereas magnesium nitride is magnesium
three N two.
Their formulas follow lithium plus one, magnesium plus two and nitride minus
three charge bookkeeping.
In ideal hydrolysis equations, one lithium nitride with three waters gives
three lithium hydroxides and one ammonia.
One magnesium nitride with six waters gives three magnesium hydroxides and two
ammonias.
Equal formula unit amounts therefore produce different ammonia amounts.
Beryllium and aluminium supply another selected diagonal comparison because
their oxides can show amphoteric behaviour.
This is resemblance in particular chemistry, not interchangeability of every
salt, reaction condition or oxidation state.
Small sizes and charge density help organize these patterns, but a simple
diagonal arrow cannot replace balanced equations.
These examples support periodic reasoning; they do not imply that every
historical s block preparation belongs to the current syllabus or that all
neighbouring diagonal pairs behave identically.
Electronegativity helps organize some acid strength trends, but it is not the
only variable.
Across the simple second period hydrogen compounds, the qualitative proton
donation tendency increases from methane through ammonia and water to hydrogen
fluoride.
Increasing attraction for electron density helps stabilize the negative
species
left after proton loss.
This compares the acid role of each hydride; ammonia can still be a base in an
ordinary reaction with water or an acid.
Down a group, changing atom size and bond strength can outweigh the
electronegativity trend.
Hydrogen chloride is a strong acid in ordinary dilute water, whereas hydrogen
fluoride is a weak acid even though fluorine is more electronegative.
The particularly strong hydrogen fluorine bond is part of the explanation;
solution stabilization must also be included in a full thermodynamic account.
Do not confuse this hydrogen halide bond comparison with the fluorine fluorine
bond in elemental fluorine.
Solvent matters, and water levels several strong acids by converting them
substantially to hydronium.
A periodic arrow therefore helps form a hypothesis, but the actual species,
solvent and proton transfer equilibrium decide the comparison.
A melting point trend across a period must be connected to the structures
actually present.
Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metallic solids, with different metallic
interactions and crystal structures.
Silicon instead has an extended covalent network, so melting requires major
disruption of a connected bonding framework.
Its high melting point cannot be explained by imagining separate silicon
molecules held together only by weak dispersion forces.
On the right side, specify the allotrope: white phosphorus contains P four
molecules, ordinary molecular sulfur contains S eight rings, and chlorine
consists of chlorine two molecules.
Their solid structures involve attractions between those molecules.
Solid argon contains individual atoms held by dispersion forces, not argon two
molecules or a covalent network.
Molecular size, polarizability and packing contribute to differences between
the molecular solids.
Melting does not normally mean breaking every covalent bond within each
phosphorus or sulfur molecule.
Nor does atomic number alone enforce a steady increase or decrease in melting
point across the period.
Use the stated elemental form, pressure and bonding category before comparing
a
property, and do not transfer the white phosphorus description to every
phosphorus allotrope.
A shorter homonuclear bond is not automatically stronger when comparing
different elements.
Elemental fluorine has a short fluorine fluorine bond, yet its dissociation
enthalpy is lower than that of chlorine chlorine.
In the usual qualitative explanation, the small fluorine atoms bring
nonbonding
electron pairs close together, and their repulsions weaken the bond.
This does not mean that every bond containing fluorine is weak: the hydrogen
fluorine bond is especially strong.
For a numerical comparison, take supplied representative gas phase
dissociation
enthalpies of one hundred fifty eight kilojoules per mole fluorine molecules
and two hundred forty three per mole chlorine molecules.
Dissociating one mole of either diatomic produces two moles of atoms.
The corresponding enthalpy per mole of atoms is therefore seventy nine for
fluorine and one hundred twenty one point five for chlorine.
Confusing a mole of molecules with a mole of atoms introduces a factor of two
error.
Bond dissociation alone also cannot rank all aqueous oxidizing strengths,
because electron gain, solvation and other steps contribute.
Specify the bond, physical state and amount basis before turning a periodic
size trend into an energy prediction.
Similar looking oxygen formulas can represent different anions.
Lithium oxide contains an oxide ion, one oxygen atom with charge minus two.
Sodium peroxide contains a peroxide unit, two oxygens sharing total charge
minus two.
Potassium superoxide contains a superoxide unit, two oxygens sharing total
charge minus one.
With the metal assigned plus one, oxygen oxidation numbers are therefore minus
two, minus one and minus one half, respectively.
The fractional superoxide value is an average oxidation number, not a claim
that an isolated oxygen atom has half an electron attached.
An oxide ion has ten total electrons; peroxide and superoxide molecular ions
have eighteen and seventeen, respectively.
In the elementary isolated oxygen ion orbital model, peroxide has all
electrons
paired whereas superoxide has one unpaired electron.
This connects charge bookkeeping to magnetic predictions without confusing an
atomic ion with a two atom ion.
These named compounds illustrate selected size and charge density trends in
alkali metal chemistry.
Actual oxygen reaction products depend on conditions and can include mixtures,
so do not turn this illustrative sequence into a guarantee that each metal
forms only one oxygen compound under every circumstance.
A periodic oxidizing trend becomes a testable electron transfer comparison
when
both half reactions are specified.
Use supplied standard reduction potentials one point three six volts for
chlorine to chloride, one point zero seven for bromine to bromide and zero
point five four for iodine accepting electrons to form the anion I
minus.
Chlorine accepting electrons while bromide loses them gives cell potential one
point three six minus one point zero seven, or plus zero point two nine volt.
The balanced net reaction is one chlorine molecule plus two bromides forming
two chlorides and one bromine molecule.
Bromine accepting electrons from iodide anions, written I minus, similarly
gives plus zero point five three volt.
Iodine oxidizing chloride instead gives zero point five four minus one point
three six, or minus zero point eight two volt, so that written direction is
not
standard thermodynamically favoured in this comparison.
Chlorine, bromine and iodine therefore form the stated descending oxidizing
sequence.
Equal amounts of gas and salt are not generally the reaction ratio: one mole
halogen consumes two moles monovalent halide.
These standard state predictions do not specify reaction speed or replace
concentration and solvent checks.
Fluorine's reaction with water prevents treating it as an interchangeable
ordinary aqueous displacement test.
A group trend must name the anion as well as the metal.
From magnesium toward barium, hydroxide solubility generally increases, while
sulfate solubility generally decreases in the usual aqueous comparison.
There is no single rule saying that every salt becomes more soluble down this
group.
Lattice separation, hydration and entropy all contribute to dissolution free
energy, and their balance depends on the compound.
Use an explicitly ideal pure water calculation for a divalent metal hydroxide,
excluding complexation, hydrolysis and water's small background contribution.
If its molar solubility is s, dissolved metal concentration is s and hydroxide
concentration twice s, giving solubility product four s cubed.
With supplied illustrative barium hydroxide constant two point five six times
ten to the minus four, the model solubility is zero point zero four zero zero
molar.
A supplied magnesium hydroxide constant one point zero eight times ten to the
minus eleven gives about one point three nine times ten to the minus four
molar
under that same model.
These concentration based results are not promises of exact measured values
when activity effects become appreciable.
Do not reuse a one to one salt's square root formula for this hydroxide
stoichiometry.
Thermal stability describes a tendency under specified conditions, not a
universal temperature printed on a formula.
Magnesium to barium carbonates generally become harder to decompose in the
usual group comparison.
The smaller divalent cation polarizes carbonate more strongly, a useful
qualitative contribution to this pattern.
Lithium carbonate is less thermally stable than the other familiar alkali
metal
carbonates and can form lithium oxide plus carbon dioxide under appropriate
conditions.
This selected exception does not make lithium divalent; its decomposition
equation contains lithium two carbonate and lithium two oxide, both with
lithium plus one.
Carbon dioxide pressure also matters.
For a divalent carbonate in equilibrium with its oxide, when both pure solids
are present, the equilibrium quotient involves carbon dioxide pressure
relative
to its standard pressure.
Increasing that pressure opposes the decomposition direction at fixed
temperature.
In a supplied complete calcium carbonate decomposition ledger, five point zero
zero grams with molar mass one hundred gives zero point zero five zero zero
mole carbon dioxide.
Its mass is two point two zero grams, leaving two point eight zero grams
calcium oxide.
The complete conversion ledger is a stipulated endpoint, not a prediction that
a closed sample must fully decompose at any temperature.
